etymology: From Middle English prauncen (to prance, to spring or bound), of uncertain further origin, possibly echoic of the sound of hooves; the plural noun form appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Deborah and Barak's victory song over Sisera.
biblical_def:
Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones.

Pransings appears once in the Authorized Version, in the Song of Deborah, Israel's oldest surviving poetry, sung after the LORD delivered Sisera's nine hundred chariots of iron into the hand of a woman and a tent-peg. The word names the violent, repeated bounding of warhorses driven to rout — not a stately parade-ground gait but the churning, broken-hoofed flight of a defeated army's cavalry, doubled in the Hebrew poetic parallelism ("the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones") for emphasis, the repetition itself mimicking the drumbeat of hooves. The mighty ones are Sisera's own charioteers, and the doubled word turns their strength into a picture of collapse: the very horses bred for war become an image of disorder and defeat when the LORD fights for His people. Judges 5 as a whole is a song built from concrete, physical details — a nail through a temple, a mother waiting at a lattice, stars fighting from heaven — and pransings belongs to that same unflinching, sensory register. It is Scripture's own war poetry, and it credits the victory to God rather than to Israel's arms, which had none worth naming against nine hundred chariots of iron.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PRANCE: to spring or bound, as a horse in high mettle; the plural noun names the repeated bounding leaps of warhorses, here in the rout of Sisera's chariotry.
webster_full: PRANCE, v.i. To spring or bound, as a horse in high mettle.
PRANCE, v.i. To ride with bounding motion; to move gaily or proudly.
PRANSINGS, n. plural. The bounding leaps of horses, here doubled for poetic emphasis.
In Judges 5:22 the word describes the broken flight of Sisera's charioteers before the LORD.
The doubling of the word in Hebrew parallelism intensifies the picture of rout and collapse.
scriptures: Jdg 5:22
Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones.
corruption_summary: A purely literary reading of Deborah's song can admire its poetry while missing that the song itself insists the victory belongs to the LORD, not to Israel's strength or strategy.
corruption_paragraphs: Taught as ancient Hebrew battle poetry alone, the verse becomes a museum piece — vivid imagery from a vanished war, safely distant from any claim on the reader. That misses that Deborah sings this song as worship, not as literature; verse 31 ends not with a boast but a prayer, "so let all thine enemies perish, O LORD."

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Deborah's own: the LORD fights for His people, and even the collapse of a mighty army's cavalry becomes material for praise rather than mere military reporting.
roots_summary: Pransings occurs once, in the doubled Hebrew parallelism of Deborah's victory song, describing the broken flight of Sisera's charioteers before the LORD's deliverance.

The word is doubled in Hebrew poetic parallelism for emphasis: 'the pransings, the pransings.'

Judges 5:31 turns the whole song toward prayer: 'so let all thine enemies perish, O LORD.'
The song credits the victory to the LORD, not to Israel's own strength or arms.

So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD (Jdg 5:31) — the song's own conclusion.
The stars in their courses fought against Sisera (Jdg 5:20) — the same battle from heaven's side.

etymology: From Old English sliht/sleaht influenced by Old Norse slettr (smooth, even), through Middle English slight (of little weight or importance); appearing twice in the Authorized Version, both times in Jeremiah's identical indictment of the false prophets and priests.
biblical_def:
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.

Slightly appears twice in the Authorized Version, in an identical refrain Jeremiah repeats against Judah's prophets and priests in Jeremiah 6:14 and again in 8:11. The word names a healing that is superficial, careless, done without weight or seriousness — a physician's bandage over a mortal wound, dressed just well enough to stop the patient asking further questions. The hurt in view is the daughter of my people, the nation's sin and coming judgment, and the false healers are those who ought to have diagnosed it truthfully but instead offered comfortable words. Their prescription is the refrain Peace, peace, spoken over a people for whom there is no peace — a false assurance mistaken for pastoral kindness. Jeremiah's repetition of the exact charge across two chapters shows this was not an isolated failure but the settled pattern of Judah's religious establishment: prophets who prophesied falsely and priests who bore rule by their means, and the LORD's people loved to have it so (Jer 5:31). Scripture measures true ministry not by the comfort it offers in the moment but by whether it names sin accurately and points toward the only remedy that actually heals.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SLIGHT: not thorough; superficial; done with little care or exertion; here of a healing applied without seriousness to a mortal wound.
webster_full: SLIGHT, adj. Not thorough; superficial; of little weight or importance.
SLIGHTLY, adv. In a slight manner; without thoroughness or care.
In Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11 the word describes a false healing that treats symptom without cause.
The refrain 'Peace, peace; when there is no peace' names the false comfort such healing offers.
Jeremiah repeats the charge verbatim across two chapters against the same failure of prophet and priest.
scriptures: Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic pastoral culture prizes making people feel better as the chief aim of ministry, precisely the slight healing Jeremiah condemns when it replaces honest diagnosis of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: A ministry philosophy built around felt needs and comfortable messaging can become the very slightly-healing pattern Jeremiah names, offering reassurance where confrontation with sin is what the moment actually requires. The test is not how a message lands but whether it tells the truth about the hurt.

The historic pastoral standard, drawn straight from this text, is that a faithful shepherd diagnoses the wound before dressing it, however unwelcome the diagnosis. The principle to recover is Jeremiah's own: Peace, peace spoken where there is no peace is not kindness but a slight healing that leaves the deeper wound to fester.

When there is no peace — the false assurance Jeremiah exposes as no healing at all.

etymology: From Middle English bad, of uncertain origin, possibly related to Old English baeddel; the abstract noun of quality appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Pharaoh's dream of the lean kine devouring the fat.
biblical_def:
Such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness.

Badness appears once in the Authorized Version, in Pharaoh's own retelling of his dream to Joseph, describing the seven lean and ill favoured kine that came up out of the river after the seven fat ones. The word names a quality of wretchedness so extreme that Pharaoh, ruler of the greatest kingdom he knew, had never seen its equal anywhere in his land. The dream is not ordinary; it is a prophetic sign, given twice in doubled form (kine and ears of corn) precisely because, as Joseph explains, the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass (Gen 41:32). The badness of the lean kine pictures the coming famine that would strip Egypt and the surrounding nations of their plenty, a famine Joseph's own God-given interpretation and God-given wisdom would prepare for fourteen years in advance. What Pharaoh could only describe as an image beyond his experience, Joseph named with precision and turned into a plan of preservation — a pattern of providence in which God reveals coming evil not to leave His people helpless before it but so that wisdom, under Him, can meet it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BAD: deficient in good qualities; the abstract noun of that deficiency, here describing the wretched leanness of Pharaoh's dream-kine.
webster_full: BAD, adj. Deficient in good qualities, physical or moral; not good.
BADNESS, n. The quality of being bad; wretchedness of condition.
In Genesis 41:19 the word describes the extreme leanness of the seven ill favoured kine.
Pharaoh's dream is doubled (kine and corn) because the matter is established by God (Gen 41:32).
Joseph's interpretation turns the dream's badness into fourteen years of prepared provision.
scriptures: And, behold, seven other kine came up after them, poor and very ill favoured and leanfleshed, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness:
corruption_summary: A reading of Joseph's rise that treats it as a self-made success story misses that the whole account turns on God revealing coming evil to a man who had first been sold into slavery and forgotten in prison.
corruption_paragraphs: Told as a rags-to-riches tale of talent and diligence rewarded, the account loses its actual center: Joseph's gift of interpretation is repeatedly credited to God alone (Gen 41:16), and the whole chain of betrayal, slavery, and imprisonment that preceded it is later named by Joseph himself as what God meant unto good (Gen 50:20).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence itself: the badness Pharaoh saw in a dream became, in God's hand, the means of preserving Egypt, Joseph's own family, and the messianic line through seven years of plenty prepared for seven years of famine.
roots_summary: Badness occurs once, describing the lean kine of Pharaoh's dream, a doubled prophetic sign that Joseph interprets as coming famine and turns into fourteen years of God-given preparation.
roots_lines: Badness in Genesis 41:19 describes the extreme wretchedness of the seven lean kine.
The dream is doubled (kine, then ears of corn) because 'the thing is established by God' (Gen 41:32).
Joseph names the badness precisely: seven years of famine following seven years of plenty.
Joseph later sums the whole account: 'ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good' (Gen 50:20).
The dream's badness becomes, in providence, the means of Egypt's and Israel's preservation.
usage: Such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness — Pharaoh's own testimony to the dream's severity.
The thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass (Gen 41:32).
Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good (Gen 50:20) — the account's own verdict on the whole matter.

etymology: From Old French balance (a pair of scales), from Latin bilanx (having two scale-pans); the plural noun appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Elihu's speech before the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind.
biblical_def:
Dost thou know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him which is perfect in knowledge?

Balancings appears once in the Authorized Version, in Elihu's final speech to Job, the last human voice before God Himself speaks out of the whirlwind. The word names the mysterious equilibrium by which clouds, heavy with water, hang suspended in the sky rather than falling — a question aimed to expose the limits of Job's knowledge against the limitlessness of God's. Elihu's whole speech in Job 36 and 37 is a rehearsal, in creation's own terms, of what God will shortly demand of Job directly: canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, knowest thou the ordinances of heaven (Job 38:31, 33). The balancings of the clouds is one item in a long catalogue — lightning, thunder, snow, ice, wind — by which Elihu argues that a man who cannot explain the physics of a rain cloud has no standing to demand an explanation from the God who set that cloud's balance. The question is not rhetorical cruelty but pastoral preparation: Job is about to meet God, and Elihu's questions soften the ground so that when the whirlwind speaks, Job's answer will be I know that thou canst do every thing (Job 42:2) rather than a further complaint.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BALANCE: equilibrium; equipoise; the plural noun here of the mysterious suspension of clouds in the sky, one of Elihu's questions rehearsing the limits of human knowledge.
webster_full: BALANCE, n. Equilibrium; equal weight or force on both sides; equipoise.
BALANCINGS, n. plural. The state or manner of being held in equilibrium.
In Job 37:16 the word names the suspension of rain-laden clouds in the sky.
Elihu's question anticipates God's own questions to Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38).
The catalogue of creation's mysteries prepares Job to answer, 'I know that thou canst do every thing' (Job 42:2).
scriptures: Dost thou know the balancings of the clouds, the wondrous works of him which is perfect in knowledge?
corruption_summary: A purely scientific reading of clouds and weather can mistake explaining a mechanism for having mastered it, missing that Elihu's question stands even after meteorology answers the physics.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern meteorology can describe the balancings of the clouds in the language of condensation, updraft, and pressure, and a confident scientism can conclude the mystery is therefore closed. Elihu's question is not defeated by an accurate mechanism; a man who can now describe how clouds are balanced still did not set the balance, still does not sustain it, and remains as dependent on the God who did as Job was.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond ordinary scientism. The principle to recover is Elihu's own: knowledge of a thing's mechanism is not the same as authority over it, and the true answer to every question about creation's balancings is worship, not mere explanation.
roots_summary: Balancings occurs once, in Elihu's catalogue of creation's mysteries, preparing Job to meet the LORD's own questions out of the whirlwind with humility rather than further complaint.

I know that thou canst do every thing (Job 42:2) — Job's answer after the whirlwind.

etymology: From Old English blaec (black) with the diminutive/approximative suffix -ish; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Job's description of the deceitful brook that fails the thirsty traveler.
biblical_def:
Which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid.

Blackish appears once in the Authorized Version, in Job's bitter complaint against his three friends, whom he compares to a wadi that runs dark and full with melted ice and snow in winter but vanishes into dry heat when travelers actually need it in summer. The word describes the water's discolored, murky appearance, darkened by the ice and snow feeding it — not clean and clear but blackish, foreshadowing that this brook cannot be trusted even at its fullest. Job's point in chapter 6 is precise and wounded: my brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away (Job 6:15), because his friends arrived full of words when he needed comfort and instead offered accusation once his suffering demanded something real of them. The troops of Tema and the companies of Sheba looked for water and were confounded because they hoped (Job 6:19-20), exactly Job's own experience of friends who promised support and delivered only disappointment. The blackish brook is one of Scripture's sharpest images for false comfort: impressive from a distance, undrinkable up close, and gone entirely when the need is greatest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLACK with the diminutive suffix -ish: somewhat black; darkish; here of ice-fed water discolored and murky, an image of unreliable comfort.
webster_full: BLACK, adj. Destitute of light; of the darkest color.
BLACKISH, adj. Somewhat black; tending toward black; darkish.
In Job 6:16 the word describes ice-melt water, dark and murky, that fails travelers in the heat of need.
Job compares his friends to this treacherous brook: full of appearance, empty of substance when tested.
The image anticipates Job 6:19-20, where travelers who hoped for the water were confounded.
scriptures: Job 6:16
Which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid:
corruption_summary: A modern reading of Job's friends can flatten them into simple villains, missing that Job's own complaint is precisely about the gap between how impressive and full comfort can look and how empty it proves when actually needed.
corruption_paragraphs: Friendship culture prizes presence and words as comfort in themselves, but Job's image warns that a brook full of ice-melt and blackish water is not the same as a brook that will still be there in the heat of true need. Job's friends are not condemned for arriving; they are condemned for what they became once his suffering required more than their words could supply.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Job's own: comfort measured by appearance in the easy season proves nothing about its reliability in the hard one, and true friendship is tested precisely where the blackish brook fails.
roots_summary: Blackish occurs once, describing the murky, ice-fed brook Job compares to his three friends — impressive when unneeded, dry and undrinkable when his suffering demanded real comfort.

The image names comfort that looks impressive but fails precisely when true need arrives.

etymology: From Old English blaesan (to blow, to puff), related to blawan (to blow); the verb blaze abroad meaning to proclaim publicly, appearing in the Authorized Version of Mark's account of the leper Jesus cleansed.
biblical_def:
But he went out, and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter.

Blaze appears in Mark's Gospel describing what the cleansed leper did after Jesus healed him and charged him, straitly, to say nothing to any man but to go show himself to the priest, according to the law of Moses, for a testimony unto them (Mark 1:44). The word names an act of loud, public, uncontainable proclamation — the opposite of the quiet, lawful obedience Jesus had commanded. Rather than going first to the priest as instructed, the man went out and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter, so that the direct consequence, recorded immediately after, is that Jesus could no more openly enter into the city, but was without in desert places: and they came to him from every quarter (Mark 1:45). The episode is one of several in Mark where Jesus commands silence — the so-called Messianic secret — precisely because premature, uncontrolled publicity threatened to provoke a response to His miracles before His identity and mission as the suffering, dying, rising Christ could be rightly understood. The cleansed man's blazing abroad was not wicked in its content (the news was true) but disobedient in its timing, a reminder that even good news told out of step with God's appointed order can hinder rather than help the very work it means to celebrate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLAZE: to publish or make known far and wide; to spread abroad by loud or public report, here of the healed leper disobeying Jesus' charge to silence.
webster_full: BLAZE, v.i. To be conspicuous; to shine, as flame; also, figuratively, to spread far and wide.
BLAZE ABROAD, v.t. To publish or make known widely, especially beyond what is warranted.
In Mark 1:45 the word describes the cleansed leper disobeying Jesus' charge to silence.
The direct result was that Jesus could no more openly enter the city, but stayed in desert places.
The episode belongs to Mark's pattern of Jesus commanding silence before His identity was rightly understood.
scriptures: Mar 1:45

But he went out, and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter, insomuch that Jesus could no more openly enter into the city, but was without in desert places: and they came to him from every quarter.
corruption_summary: A modern reading that measures ministry success by publicity and reach alone can miss that Scripture here shows uncontrolled proclamation, even of a true miracle, working directly against Christ's own appointed timing and purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that prizes going viral above obedience can read the cleansed leper's enthusiasm as simply admirable zeal, missing that Jesus had given him a specific, lawful instruction he directly disobeyed. Good news shared out of step with God's order is not automatically good discipleship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Mark's own narrative judgment: the leper's blazing abroad, however well-intentioned, hindered rather than helped Christ's work in that season, a caution against confusing enthusiasm with obedience.

etymology: From Old French bleu, of Germanic origin, related to Old High German blao; the abstract noun of color appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Proverbs' teaching on physical correction.
biblical_def:
The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so do stripes the inward parts of the belly.

Blueness appears once in the Authorized Version, describing the bruised, discolored mark left by a physical blow — the visible sign of a stripe or wound. Proverbs 20:30 sets this alongside its parallel line, so do stripes the inward parts of the belly, to make a single, difficult point: physical correction, painful and disfiguring on the surface, can reach and cleanse what lighter measures cannot touch, penetrating to the inward parts. The verse belongs to a cluster of Proverbs on the discipline of the fool and the wayward, alongside the rod that drives out the foolishness bound in the heart of a child (Pro 22:15) and correction that delivereth his soul from hell (Pro 23:14). Wisdom literature does not romanticize the blueness itself; it is a real bruise, a real cost, and the book elsewhere prizes gentleness, a soft answer, and the tongue of the wise as health (Pro 15:1, 4). But Proverbs refuses the sentimental notion that correction must always be painless to be loving, insisting instead that some evil is cleansed only by a discipline severe enough to leave a mark, administered rightly and for the sinner's own good, not by cruelty for its own sake.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLUE: the abstract noun of that color, here of a bruise or livid mark left by a blow, used in Proverbs of the deep-reaching effect of physical correction.
webster_full: BLUE, adj. A color resembling that of the clear sky; also, livid, as a bruise.
BLUENESS, n. The quality or state of being blue; here of a bruise's discoloration.
In Proverbs 20:30 the word names the visible mark of a stripe, paired with 'stripes the inward parts of the belly.'
The verse belongs to Proverbs' wider teaching on the discipline of the fool (Pro 22:15).
Wisdom literature pairs such severity with equal praise of gentleness and the soft answer (Pro 15:1).
scriptures: The blueness of a wound cleanseth away evil: so do stripes the inward parts of the belly.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic culture that treats all pain as harm by definition struggles with Proverbs' plain claim that some correction cleanses precisely because it is severe, and can either soften the text past recognition or weaponize it past what Scripture's own balance allows.
corruption_paragraphs: A reading that either explains away the verse's plain sense to avoid discomfort, or isolates it from Proverbs' equal insistence on gentleness and the soft answer (Pro 15:1), both miss the book's actual balance: real correction, rightly administered, for real ends, held together with real tenderness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond therapeutic softening. The principle to recover is wisdom literature's own balance: discipline is not opposed to love but can be one of its instruments, provided it serves the disciplined one's soul rather than the discipliner's anger.
roots_summary: Blueness occurs once, in Proverbs' teaching that physical correction, painful and disfiguring on the surface, can reach and cleanse what lighter measures cannot, held in balance with the book's equal praise of gentleness.

Proverbs 22:15 makes the same point of children: 'the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.'
Proverbs 23:14 states the purpose: correction 'shalt deliver his soul from hell.'
Proverbs 15:1 balances the whole with equal weight: 'a soft answer turneth away wrath.'

The rod of correction shall drive it far from him (Pro 22:15).
A soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1) — wisdom's own balancing word.

etymology: From Middle English blunt, of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Old Norse blundra (to shut the eyes, to doze); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Preacher's teaching on wisdom and preparation.
biblical_def:
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.

Blunt appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ecclesiastes' practical wisdom about an axe or tool whose edge has grown dull through use. The Preacher's observation is deliberately homely: a blunt iron still cuts, but at a cost — more strength must be put to it, more exertion for the same result a sharp edge would achieve with ease. The lesson he draws is not about tools at all but about wisdom itself, profitable to direct, the very quality that would have told the woodsman to stop and sharpen before continuing rather than grinding on through sheer force. Ecclesiastes as a whole examines labor under the sun and repeatedly finds that skill, timing, and wisdom matter more than raw effort; a little earlier the Preacher has already observed that if the axe head fall into the water, borrowed strength cannot retrieve wisdom lost by carelessness (implied by 10:9-10's warning about handling stones and cleaving wood without care). The blunt iron is Ecclesiastes' small, concrete parable for a larger truth: unreflective effort, however strenuous, is no substitute for the wisdom to prepare well before the labor begins.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from BLUNT: dull; not sharp; having a thick edge or point; here of a tool requiring extra strength because its edge was not first sharpened.
webster_full: BLUNT, adj. Having a thick edge or point; not sharp.
BLUNT, adj. figuratively: dull in perception; not quick or acute.
In Ecclesiastes 10:10 the word describes an axe iron whose dullness costs the workman extra strength.
The Preacher's point is practical: 'wisdom is profitable to direct,' preparing before the labor begins.
The verse belongs to Ecclesiastes' wider theme that skill and timing outweigh raw effort under the sun.
scriptures: If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.
corruption_summary: A culture that prizes hustle and raw effort as virtues in themselves can miss Ecclesiastes' plainer point, that unreflective labor without the wisdom to prepare well is simply harder than it needs to be, not more godly for the extra strain.
corruption_paragraphs: A grind-culture reading of work can treat exhaustion itself as proof of diligence, exactly the blunt-iron approach the Preacher gently corrects: more strength spent on a dull edge is not virtue but a failure to first sharpen the tool.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Preacher's own: wisdom is profitable to direct, and preparing well before labor honors the work far more than sheer exertion applied to a blunt and unready edge.
roots_summary: Blunt occurs once, in Ecclesiastes' homely parable of a dull axe iron, teaching that wisdom to prepare before labor outweighs raw strength applied without it.

The cost of the dullness is measured in extra strength the workman must supply.

The verse belongs to Ecclesiastes' wider theme of labor and skill 'under the sun' (Ecc 2:24).
The parable teaches that preparation, not raw exertion, is wisdom's true mark in ordinary work.
usage: If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength.
But wisdom is profitable to direct (Ecc 10:10) — the Preacher's own conclusion.
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might (Ecc 9:10) — effort still matters, rightly directed.

etymology: From Old English brecan (to break), the plural noun of the act or effect of breaking; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the LORD's description of leviathan's terrifying power.
biblical_def:
When he raiseth up himself, the mighty are afraid: by reason of breakings they purify themselves.

Breakings appears once in the Authorized Version, in the LORD's long description of leviathan near the close of His answer to Job out of the whirlwind. The word names the shattering, destructive effect leviathan's rising causes among even the mighty — strong men so terrified by the creature's power that, in the older sense the verse carries, they purify or beside themselves with fear lose composure entirely at the mere breakings, the consequences of leviathan's movement. Job 41 belongs to God's final and most overwhelming demonstration to Job: if a mere creature, however fearsome, can undo the courage of mighty men, how much less can Job stand in judgment over the One who made and governs that creature. The chapter follows behemoth in Job 40 as the second half of a pair, both creatures functioning less as zoological curiosities than as living arguments — embodiments of power no man can tame, presented to silence a man who had demanded an audience with God to plead his case. The breakings leviathan causes are a small picture of a larger truth the whole book drives toward: Job's proper posture before such power is not explanation but the answer he finally gives, I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2).

corruption_summary: A purely zoological curiosity about leviathan's identity can distract from the text's actual purpose, which is to humble Job's demand for an explanation by confronting him with power that exceeds his own beyond measure.
corruption_paragraphs: Debating whether leviathan names a crocodile, a whale, or a mythic sea-dragon can absorb attention the text itself does not spend that way; Job 41 is far more interested in what the creature's power proves about its Maker than in a zoological catalogue entry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the whole speech's aim: if leviathan's mere rising breaks the courage of mighty men, Job's proper answer to God is not further argument but worship, exactly the posture Job takes up in Job 42:2-6.

etymology: From Old English bredan (to nourish, to bring forth), the past tense of breed; appearing in the Authorized Version of the manna narrative in Exodus, describing what happened when Israel disobeyed Moses' instruction.
biblical_def:
Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank.

Bred appears in Exodus, in the account of Israel's first days receiving manna in the wilderness, when Moses instructed the people to gather only what they needed for that day and to leave none of it till the morning (Exo 16:19). Some of the people disregarded the instruction, kept a portion overnight, and found in the morning that it had bred worms and stank — a small, physical, unmistakable sign of disobedience made visible. The manna was itself a daily lesson in dependence: bread from heaven, given fresh each morning, teaching Israel that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD (Deu 8:3), a lesson Christ Himself would later apply against Satan in the wilderness (Mat 4:4). The corruption of the hoarded manna was not an accident of climate but a built-in consequence of grasping today for a provision God intended to give again tomorrow, exactly as He had promised. The episode stands as one of Scripture's clearest pictures of daily dependence versus anxious hoarding, later echoed in Christ's own teaching to pray give us this day our daily bread (Mat 6:11) rather than to lay up treasures against an imagined future scarcity God has not promised to withhold.

BRED, v. The past tense and participle of breed; produced, generated.

The episode teaches daily dependence on God's provision rather than anxious hoarding against the future.
scriptures: Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank: and Moses was wroth with them.
corruption_summary: A self-reliant modern instinct treats saving and stockpiling as unqualified virtues, missing that Scripture's manna narrative specifically condemns hoarding what God had promised to supply again, fresh, the very next day.
corruption_paragraphs: General prudence and disobedient hoarding are not the same category, but a reading that flattens all saving into wisdom can miss that this particular provision came with an explicit command not to keep it overnight, precisely to teach daily trust rather than self-sufficient stockpiling.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's own application of daily dependence: give us this day our daily bread (Mat 6:11), asked fresh each day rather than assumed as a stockpile already secured by human effort alone.
